newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai politicians switch camps ahead of polls.
newsitem.headline: Thai politicians switch camps ahead of polls.

text.p: The ranks of Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's New Aspiration Party (NAP) have been swelled by defecting members of parliament, boosting its chances in the forthcoming elections, political sources said on Wednesday.
A top official of outgoing Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa's Chart Thai party said he had defected to the NAP and claimed he had taken about 30 MPs with him.
The small Nam Thai party, led by Foreign Minister Amnuay Viravan, said it would be disbanded from Wednesday and 16 of its 18 MPs would join the NAP.
Chavalit confirmed the latest additions to his party's ranks and said he expected more to join.
"We are accepting everyone who shares a similar ideology. The NAP will be the chain to link the past to the future," he said in a television interview.
Political analysts said the NAP's chances in the elections set for November 17 had strengthened as a result of the defections from the Chart Thai and the Nam Thai parties.
The NAP was the second largest party in Banharn's ruling coalition and controls 57 of the 391 seats in parliament.
"I was not treated properly in the Chart Thai party. So I resigned am now a member of New Aspiration Party," said Sanoh Tienthong, former secretary general of Chart Thai.

Barnharn's decision last week to dissolve parliament and call elections angered Sanoh and Chavalit. They had expected Banharn to quit, leaving the way clear for Chavalit to be named premier and head the ruling six-party coalition.
Banharn, who surprised everybody with his call for elections, is now caretaker prime minister.
Nam Thai's Amnuay, a technocrat and former banker, said he had quit politics.
"I am tired and fed up with politics. I will not run in the upcoming election and most of my party members will go to the NAP," he told reporters.
But a leader of the main opposition Democract Party said the NAP should not be over-optimistic, as defecting MPs often lost when they stood for re-election.
"Dont be over-optimistic, because the lesson in the past is that defectors fail to get re-elected to parliament," said Abhisit Vejajiva, Democrat party spokesman.
The Democrats won 86 seats in last July's elections. Party sources said it expected to gain 11 more MPs through defections from the small Seritham party.
